core: Balance as the design principle governing the distribution of visual weight so a composition feels stable or intentionally unstable
Visual weight and the factors that create it: size, color (hue and saturation), value/darkness, complexity/detail, position/distance from center, and isolation
Symmetrical (formal) balance: equal weights mirrored across a central axis; orderly, stable, can feel static
Asymmetrical (informal) balance: unequal weights offset without mirroring; dynamic, supports a focal point
Radial balance: elements radiating from a central point, even weight on all sides, strong central focal point
Mosaic / crystallographic / all-over balance: weight spread so evenly that no focal point emerges
Deliberate imbalance to create visual tension when it serves the message
supporting: Balance is a perceptual judgment tested and felt rather than measured
Approximate symmetry as a middle ground between exact mirror symmetry and asymmetry
How rebalancing interacts with contrast and visual hierarchy since the same size/color choices drive all three

claims.claim: Balance is the design principle concerned with the distribution of visual weight across a composition; a design feels balanced when the visual weights on and around a central axis are roughly equivalent.

Visual weight is the amount of attention an element attracts, and it is increased by larger size, brighter and more saturated color, darker value, greater contrast, more complexity or detail, and by isolating an element in empty space.

Symmetrical balance places equal visual weights in matching positions on either side of a central axis so one half mirrors the other; it reads as formal and stable and is sometimes called formal balance, but can feel static.

Asymmetrical balance arranges elements of unequal weight so their differing weights still even out without mirroring; it is more dynamic than symmetry and lets a designer build a focal point, and it is sometimes called informal balance.
Radial balance arranges visual elements so they radiate outward from a central point with equal weight on all sides, producing a strong focal point at the center.

Mosaic balance, also called crystallographic or all-over balance, spreads visual weight so evenly across the whole surface that the composition has no single focal point, achieving balance through repetition rather than symmetry or offsetting weights.
An intentionally unbalanced composition creates visual tension, which can be the right choice when instability supports the message being communicated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the terms 'formal' and 'informal' balance are standard names for symmetrical and asymmetrical balance
positions: The Smashing Magazine article notes symmetrical balance is sometimes called formal balance
The LibreTexts OER by Rodenhauser uses only 'symmetrical', 'asymmetrical', and 'radial' and does not use 'formal'/'informal'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented 'formal' and 'informal' as common alternative names rather than as universal terminology, and did not attribute them to a source that does not use them.
